headline: The Rock Creek teahouse pushed out its Black operator
fact: In 1920, Hattie L. Sewell, a woman of color, won the concession to operate the Peirce Mill teahouse in Rock Creek Park. Although her business was successful, complaints from park neighbors and estate trustees led management to refuse her a new contract.
takeaway: In segregated-era DC, running a successful business did not guarantee a Black entrepreneur a fair opportunity to keep it.
source_name: National Park Service — History of Peirce Mill

headline: The Beatles' first U.S. concert happened in DC
fact: On February 11, 1964, two days after appearing on The Ed Sullivan Show, the Beatles performed their first U.S. concert at Washington Coliseum, the former Uline Arena in Northeast DC.
takeaway: Beatlemania's American concert history began in a DC neighborhood, not New York or Los Angeles.
source_name: DC Office of Planning — Ward 6 Heritage Guide

headline: The Black queer club that held space for 50 years
fact: Opened around 1953 in Columbia Heights, Nob Hill began as an upscale private club for Black gay and bisexual men. When it closed in 2004, it was DC's oldest continuously operating queer bar of color.
takeaway: For roughly half a century, a neighborhood bar gave Black queer Washingtonians a rare place to gather, celebrate, and build community.
source_name: DC Historic Preservation Office — Washington's LGBTQ Historic Context

headline: The Anacostia festival that drew 50,000 people
fact: Beginning in 1972, Malcolm X Day in Anacostia Park grew into the nation's oldest and largest tribute to Malcolm X. At its peak, the celebration drew 30,000 to 50,000 people annually for Pan-African speakers, vendors, and performances by go-go legends.
takeaway: Southeast DC created a massive homegrown festival where Black thought, music, commerce, and community moved together.
source_name: National Park Service — Malcolm X Day at Anacostia Park

headline: The school Black America built for its daughters
fact: In 1909, Nannie Helen Burroughs opened the National Training School for Women and Girls in Lincoln Heights, combining academic and vocational education for Black women and girls.
takeaway: A nationally significant education model was built in Northeast DC through Black leadership and community-funded determination.
source_name: DC Historic Preservation Office — National Training School Historic Landmark Nomination
source_quote: National Training School for Women and Girls

headline: America's first Black YMCA was born in DC
fact: In 1853, Anthony Bowen founded the nation's first African American YMCA in Washington. Its landmark Twelfth Street building later became a model for Black YMCAs nationwide.
takeaway: Black DC created a community institution for housing, education, recreation, and organizing, then supplied a blueprint other cities followed.
source_name: National Park Service — Twelfth Street YMCA

headline: The Georgetown lab that funded a Deaf library
fact: Alexander Graham Bell used France's Volta Prize money to establish a sound-research laboratory in Georgetown. After the laboratory sold its recording patents in 1887, Bell used his profits to found the Volta Bureau, a library serving Deaf people and deafness researchers.
takeaway: A DC laboratory turned early recording technology into lasting support for Deaf education and access.

headline: A DC scientist's camera is still sitting on the Moon
fact: In 1972, Naval Research Laboratory scientist George Carruthers' 50-pound, gold-plated camera became the first observatory based on the Moon. It captured humanity's first ultraviolet photographs of Earth from the lunar surface and remains on the Moon today.
takeaway: A breakthrough created by one of DC's Fantastic people permanently changed how humanity sees its own planet.
source_name: U.S. Naval Research Laboratory — Dr. George Carruthers' Legacy
